opus-5.5.text:
I think I was genuinely lucky, and I don't want to frame it as if I had some grand plan from the beginning. A lot of it came down to meeting the right people at the right time.

During my undergraduate years at Shanghai Jiao Tong, being in an environment like the ACM class meant I was surrounded by people who took research seriously very early. It wasn't so much that someone handed me a roadmap. It was more that the atmosphere set a standard: you should care about real problems, not just grades or getting a paper accepted. That kind of implicit guidance shapes your taste before you even realize it.

Then in my PhD with Zhuowen Tu at UCSD, and later working with people like Kaiming He at FAIR, what I learned most wasn't a specific technique. It was judgment: what's worth working on, what's a dead end, when an idea is simple but deep versus simple and shallow. Kaiming, for example, has this way of stripping a problem down until only the essential part is left. When you see someone do that repeatedly, you start to internalize it. That probably saved me from a lot of detours, like chasing complicated methods that squeeze out half a point on a benchmark and don't really matter.

But I'd add something. Avoiding detours isn't always the goal. Some of the "detours" I did take, the projects that didn't work or the directions that felt unfashionable, ended up being where I learned the most. Good guidance doesn't remove all the wandering. It helps you wander with better questions in mind, so when you do go off the main road, you come back with something.

So how do I view it now? Mostly with gratitude, and also with a sense of responsibility. Now that I'm advising students myself, I think a lot about what to pass on. I try not to tell them exactly what to do. I'd rather help them build their own taste, the way my mentors did for me, so they can tell for themselves which detours are worth taking.

r001.rationale: The response describes implicit guidance from the research environment and mentors, but does not say that guidance that seems like common sense may not be obvious to students.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I was genuinely lucky, and I don't want to dress that up as something I earned. When I was doing my PhD at UC San Diego, my advisor Zhuowen Tu gave me a kind of guidance that wasn't really about telling me what to work on. It was more about taste. He'd push back when I was chasing something because it was fashionable, and he'd ask very simple questions like, why does this matter in five years? At the time that felt frustrating, because you're a student and you want to publish, you want to show progress. But looking back, those questions saved me a lot of time. The field moves so fast that if you don't have some internal compass, you end up spending years on things that evaporate.

The second thing that mattered was the environment at FAIR after I joined. Working with people like Kaiming He, you learn by watching how they think, not by being told. Kaiming has this habit of stripping a problem down until there's almost nothing left, and then asking whether the thing that remains is actually the point. ResNeXt came out of that kind of discipline. We weren't trying to be clever. We were trying to find the one variable that mattered and hold everything else fixed. That's a very different mindset from the one most students start with, where you stack ten ideas together and hope the combination works.

So when people ask about avoiding detours, I'd be a bit careful. I did take detours. Some of them were useful, because you learn what a dead end feels like from the inside. What the good guidance did was shorten the detours, not eliminate them. Someone would say, I think you've learned what you needed to learn here, maybe it's time to move on. That kind of permission to stop is underrated. A lot of young researchers don't need to be told what to do. They need someone they trust to tell them when to let go.

And honestly, the most valuable advice was often almost embarrassingly simple. Read the old papers. Run the baseline yourself before you believe the number in the table. Don't trust a result until you've broken it at least once. None of that sounds profound, but if you actually do it consistently, it compounds over a decade.

r001.rationale: The response calls the advice “almost embarrassingly simple” and says it does not sound profound, but it does not clearly say that such guidance may be non-obvious to students.

astra-6.text:
I think that kind of guidance is incredibly valuable, especially early on, when you don’t yet have a good sense of which questions are worth pursuing. Someone more experienced can help you step back and ask, “Why does this matter? What are you actually trying to understand?” That can save you a lot of effort.

But I wouldn’t say the goal is to avoid every detour. Sometimes you have to try something that doesn’t work to develop your own judgment. The most useful guidance gives you direction while leaving you room to explore. And looking back, I think it’s important to recognize how much that support matters, rather than attributing everything to your own decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says early-career people may not know which questions are worth pursuing, but it does not clearly state that guidance that seems like common sense may not be obvious to students.

sol-6.1.text:
I think good guidance early on can be incredibly valuable, but I wouldn’t describe it as someone handing you a map so you never take a wrong turn. It’s more about helping you develop judgment: what questions are worth asking, what assumptions you should challenge, and when you need to step back and rethink your approach.

When you’re starting out, you don’t necessarily know how to distinguish a difficult problem from a problem that isn’t worth pursuing. An experienced person can help you see that distinction. But you still have to do the work and make decisions yourself. Some detours are useful—you learn something from them that advice alone couldn’t teach you. So what I appreciate most is guidance that gives you perspective while leaving you room to explore.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how experienced people help beginners judge which problems to pursue, but it does not say that guidance seeming like common sense may not be obvious to students.
